title: Pentagon says it will do what it must if it feels it can’t rely on Canada’s military
html:
Canadian Armed Forces Leopard 2A4 tanks are shown at CFB Gagetown in Oromocto, N.B., in September 2012.David Smith/The Canadian Press

The Trump administration is prepared to take significant measures if Canada does not step up its military spending, a senior Pentagon official has warned.

The official did not specify what action is being contemplated but said the intention would be to compensate for Canada’s failure to spend enough on North American continental defence.

The warning came in a briefing for Canadian reporters in Washington this week with two Pentagon officials. The Globe and Mail is not naming them as a condition of taking part in the briefing.

The U.S. government has in recent days ramped up an ongoing pressure campaign to get Ottawa to spend more on its military, including by purchasing American-made F-35 fighter jets.

Two weeks ago, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote a memo putting restrictions on U.S. military officials engaging with their Canadian counterparts. And earlier this week, the Pentagon released a “fact sheet” accusing Canada’s military of being woefully underprepared.

Mr. Hegseth’s memo is relatively limited in scope. The second official at the briefing said it effectively mandates that, if Pentagon personnel want to attend Canadian events − at Ottawa’s embassy in Washington, for instance − they now must run it by the department’s policy office so military brass can ensure it helps advance U.S. government objectives.

But the first official said the Pentagon will look at enacting other, more significant measures if it feels the U.S. can’t rely on Canada to do its part on defence.

U.S. President Donald Trump has long complained that Canada and other NATO countries spend too little on their militaries. He has threatened to annex Canada as America’s 51st state and seize control of Greenland, an autonomous Danish territory, nearly causing an unprecedented rupture in the Western defence alliance.

In response, Prime Minister Mark Carney increased defence spending to 2 per cent of GDP this year – fulfilling a commitment Canada made in 2006 – and agreed to Mr. Trump’s new NATO target of spending 5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035.

The Prime Minister has also launched talks to join Mr. Trump’s planned Golden Dome missile defence shield. Denmark and Greenland, meanwhile, signed a treaty with the U.S. spelling out Washington’s ability to expand its military installations in the territory.

But the Trump administration has accused Mr. Carney of not putting forward a concrete plan for reaching the 2035 spending target. And it has taken umbrage at the Prime Minister’s decision to review a planned purchase of F-35s from Lockheed Martin. Mr. Carney put the purchase on hold last year after Mr. Trump made his annexation threats and imposed punishing tariffs on Canada.

During the briefing, the first Pentagon official cited the F-35 purchase as one thing the administration wants to see from Canada. The official said Canada was too focused on trade issues.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Defence Minister David McGuinty wrote that “Canadians and Americans are safer when we stand together” and said Ottawa would meet its 2035 goal.

“The close defence cooperation between Canada and the United States continues,” Simon Lafortune wrote in an e-mail. “Canada will continue to do its part to defend North America as we keep having constructive discussions with our American partners on how best to strengthen our shared defence and security.”

The first Pentagon official said Canada had made modest progress on defence and that Washington had heard encouraging things from top Canadian officials, including Mark Wiseman, Canada’s ambassador in Washington. But the official said Canadian spending on defence is still far below what is needed for the U.S. to have much confidence in one of its closest allies.

Mr. Carney has tied defence and trade together, campaigning in last year’s election on a promise to seek a comprehensive commercial and security deal with the U.S.

The Globe reported this summer that, amid trade talks, the two governments had also discussed the F-35 purchase, Canada buying U.S.-made radar planes as part of joining the Golden Dome and American access to Canadian critical minerals.

Trade talks unravelled in August but have resumed in recent weeks. While both sides have said negotiations are moving forward, neither has made clear exactly how close they are to a deal.
summary: Officials say Ottawa is too focused on trade issues and not committed to increasing defence spending
